newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norske Skog profits hit by low newsprint prices.
newsitem.headline: Norske Skog profits hit by low newsprint prices.

text.p: Norwegian forestry group Norske Skogindustrier ASA on Thursday blamed lower prices for printing paper and a 100 million crown ($15.7 million) restructuring charge for a 46 percent slump in third-quarter operating profits versus the second quarter.
The company forecast profits in the fourth quarter to weaken further mainly due to stiff competition in its main market for printing paper in Europe.
Skog posted third-quarter operating profits of 289 million crowns ($45.5 million) compared with 539 million crowns in the second quarter and 699 million in the third quarter 1995.
For the first nine months, operating profits slipped seven percent to 1.48 billion crowns, versus 1.59 billion crowns a year ago, while pre-tax profits fell 10 percent to 1.32 billion crowns.

"It has been possible to maintain a satisfactory result so far this year because printing paper has provided a good profit, which has offset the very poor profitability of fibre and building materials," the company said in a statement.

"Market conditions for...printing paper have gradually weakened during the year. During the final quarter profits are expected to weaken compared with the previous months mainly owing to keener competition, in Europe, from Canadian and Russian newsprint suppliers."

Third-quarter operating profits for Skog's paper mills dropped 32 percent to 391 million crowns from 572 million crowns in the second quarter. The group took a 100 million crown cost for restructuring related to the Sande Paper Mill.

Skog said it had adjusted production at newsprint mills in view of price pressure in Europe owing to increased deliveries from Canada due to lower consumption and falling prices in the United States during 1996.
Low prices for LWC magazine paper had led to pressure in the SC magazine paper market and prices for the second half of the year had been adjusted downwards, it said.
In the fibre division nine-month operating results swung into a 105 million crown loss, against a 495 million profit in the corresponding 1995 period.

"The marked deterioration in the result compared with last year reflects the fact that pulp prices fell during the first half year from a peak of $925-1,000 per tonne, for bleached, long-fibre sulphate pulp, to $500 per tonne," Skog said.
Since July prices had risen again and reached $560-570 by the end of the thrid quarter. Skog said the outlook for market pulp was uncertain despite improved demand for fine paper.

Operating procfit for building materials tumbled to 13 million crowns in the first nine months, against 95 million, mainly reflecting a sharp decline in export prices for sawn timber since the second hald of 1995.
Skog said the balance between supply and demand for sawn timber had now improved and the market appeared to be developing favourably.
